To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) it is possible to learn a mapping from one visual domain to another using Generative Adverserial Networks (GANs) without requiring instance-to-instance correspondences; (2) this mapping allows for the generation of novel images that are perceptually plausible in the target domain; and (3) the mapping allows for the learning of a meaningful feature space in which the distances between images correspond to visual similarity, and which can be used to solve the place recognition problem across visual domains.
Generative Adverserial Networks can be used to learn meaningful feature spaces for challenging place recognition tasks, such as recognizing places under severe appearance change.
Generative Adversial Networks can be used to learn a mapping between two domains, such as winter and summer, without knowing the instance to instance correspondences.
